name: Maestri
tagline: A consumer app positioned around guided practice and mastery, sold as a subscription.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Public detail on this one is thin, so treat the reasoning as structural rather than specific. Apps in the guided-practice bracket split cleanly in two: the part that tracks what you did, and the part that tells you what to do next. The tracking half, sessions, streaks, goals, progress charts, reminders, is genuinely a one-sitting build and an agent will nail it. The instructional half, curated drills, expert-authored programs, video or audio content, is not something you generate, it is something someone wrote and licensed. Build the scaffolding yourself and supply your own curriculum, and you get most of the daily utility; expect to miss the content and the polish.
coreLoopDIY: A local practice tracker where you define skills and drill programs, log timed sessions against them, and see streaks plus per-skill progress over time.
requirements: Node 20 and a local machine or small VPS
Your own practice material: drills, exercises, or a program you already follow
Optional: a browser you keep open on a phone, since there is no native app
whatYouLose: Curated, expert-authored practice programs that you would otherwise have to design yourself
A real native mobile app with offline logging and push reminders
Any built-in audio, video, or reference material
Whatever adaptive logic decides what you practice next, instead of you deciding
Design polish, which matters more than usual for an app you are supposed to open daily
moatNotes: The defensible asset in this category is almost never the software, it is who wrote the exercises and whether you trust them.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the hard part of deliberate practice is not recording that you practiced, it is knowing what to practice, in what order, for how long. People pay to outsource that judgment to someone who has structured it before, and they pay again for the small frictionless things: a phone app that opens in a second, a notification at the right hour, a progress view that feels good enough to keep looking at. A self-built tracker gives you the ledger and leaves the curriculum entirely on you, which is fine if you already have one and useless if you do not.
notes: Thin public information, so this entry is about the shape of the category rather than this specific app.
prompt:
Build a local-first practice tracker web app in an empty folder. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable: Next.js 14 App Router with TypeScript, Tailwind, and SQLite via better-sqlite3. Single process, runs with npm run dev, data in ./data/practice.db. No auth, no external APIs, no analytics.

Data model:
- skill: id, name, color, target_minutes_per_week, archived
- drill: id, skill_id, name, description, default_minutes, order_index
- session: id, drill_id, started_at, minutes, rating 1-5, notes

Screens:
1. Today: list of drills grouped by skill, each with a start button that opens a timer. Timer counts up, pause and resume, and on stop asks for a 1-5 rating and an optional note, then writes a session.
2. Skills: CRUD for skills and their drills, drag-free reordering via up and down buttons. Keep it boring.
3. History: a calendar heatmap of total minutes per day for the last 12 weeks, plus a filterable session list.
4. Progress: per-skill weekly minutes versus target, rendered as simple bar charts. Use a tiny chart lib or raw SVG, your call, but pick one and do not add a settings page for it.

Requirements:
- Server actions for all writes, no separate API layer.
- Seed script that inserts two example skills with three drills each so the app is not empty on first run.
- JSON export and import of the whole database from a Settings route, because the user owns this data.
- Mobile-first layout, large tap targets, works fine as a browser tab on a phone.

Explicitly out of scope: push notifications, native apps, multi-user, sharing, any built-in lesson content, AI recommendations of what to practice next.

Write a README with setup, the data model, and one honest paragraph on what this does not do.
